record.original_question: A numerical semigroup Gamma is called cyclotomic if the polynomial P_Gamma(z) determined by the Hilbert series H_Gamma(z) = P_Gamma(z)/(1-z) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials. Is a numerical semigroup a complete intersection if and only if it is cyclotomic?

evidence.quote: A semigroup Γ is called cyclotomic if PΓ (z) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials. ... Problem 27 ([CGSM16, Conjecture 1]). A numerical semigroup is a complete intersection if and only if it is cyclotomic.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. Its Hilbert series is
$$H_\Gamma(z) = \sum_{n \in \Gamma} z^n,$$
which can be written uniquely in the form
$$H_\Gamma(z) = \frac{P_\Gamma(z)}{1-z}$$
for a polynomial $P_\Gamma(z) \in \mathbb{Z}[z]$ (the semigroup polynomial). The semigroup $\Gamma$ is called cyclotomic if $P_\Gamma(z)$ factors as a product of cyclotomic polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}[z]$.

A numerical semigroup $\Gamma$, minimally generated by $n_1,\dots,n_e$, is called a complete intersection if the kernel of the surjection $k[x_1,\dots,x_e] \to k[\Gamma]$ sending $x_i \mapsto t^{n_i}$ is generated by exactly $e-1$ elements (equivalently, the defining toric ideal of $\Gamma$ is a complete intersection).

Prove or disprove: a numerical semigroup is a complete intersection if and only if it is cyclotomic.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture was posed by Ciolan, García-Sánchez, and Moree (2016). One direction (complete intersection implies cyclotomic) is known. The converse remains open in general, but partial results have been established: it has been proved for semigroup polynomials with at most two irreducible factors, for certain cyclotomic exponent sequences, and verified computationally for Frobenius number up to 70.
